title: Part IX — JOURNEYS: One Order, End to End
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-13 from the published page (posts/part-9-intro/index.md, 509 words, ten units) and its former spec.md, then reordered the same day from the flow rubric (see decision_log); the page was revised to match. One spec paragraph per unit of the page; the KEY POINTS callout and Figure 3 (the before-Waypoint comparison) are evidence of the claim paragraph (p04), Figure 1 (the relay) of p01 and Figure 2 (four journeys, one chain) of p02.

know: Part IX follows four journeys in order: a consumer purchase from search to accounting, the same jacket coming back as an exchange, a retail chain's EDI reorder through order, pallet notice, invoice and payment, and a Black Friday evening followed by the next year's plan.

The first three replay April 2027 orders through the late-2027 Waypoint design (an availability service, an OMS, a PIM, and warehouse packing records for wholesale notices), keeping their dates and amounts, and compare each with the earlier landscape; the peak chapter reconstructs the 2026 incident and then presents the 2027 plan.
An order is a chain of promises, each with one owner: many systems holding a piece of one order is normal, a fact with two writers is not, and every join needs a key and a daily reconciliation.
can_do: Pick the Part IX journey that matches the order, return, business order or peak they need to trace.

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture (engineers, product managers and leaders) who have read Parts I to VIII and are about to start the journeys, or who arrive with one order, return, wholesale order or peak to trace and want the journey that matches it.
already_knows: What buying something online is like from the shopper's side.
Roughly what an API, a database and a queue are.

Part I: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines (money, goods, returns), system of record, single writer, events, idempotency and reconciliation; the glosses for PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, SKU, channel, 3PL, OMS, availability service, PIM, D2C and B2B.

Parts II to VIII: each capability, join and rule taught separately (catalog, price, stock, checkout, payment, order record, invoice, warehouse, shipping, returns, B2B and EDI, integration, security, privacy, regulation).

Kestrel & Pine in outline: a fictional outdoor brand, its systems, its incidents (among them the Three-Status Order, the Double Refund, the ASN Chargeback and the Black Friday Oversell), Bergzicht Outdoor as its largest wholesale customer and the Waypoint program; Eva's jacket order of 13 April 2027 as the book's worked order.
does_not_know: The step table, the entity–owner table and the handoff requirements as one chapter shape (introduced here, taught in journey-consumer-order).
The despatch advice's details and the four-way match (owned by journey-wholesale-order; 'pallet notice' is used here).

The reader looks at the handoffs: which system owns each fact, whether a fact has two writers, and whether each message carries an idempotency key with a daily reconciliation behind the events.

thesis.question: What do four complete journeys through the same systems show about where commerce promises break, and what keeps them?
thesis.claim: An order, its return, a wholesale reorder and a peak evening cross one chain of systems, each keeping a different promise. On Kestrel & Pine's January 2027 landscape (Black Friday 2026 for the peak) every journey broke at a handoff, not inside a system; each holds when every fact has one writer and every handoff carries an idempotency key, moves by event or daily batch as its promise's clock requires, and is reconciled.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that commerce failures are defects inside a system, so that a merchant which picks a strong product for each slot (shop platform, warehouse system, ERP, returns app) and keeps each running has a working landscape, and an order's journey is simply the sum of its steps.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim reviews its landscape by walking orders through it rather than by grading products, and spends on owners, keys, gauges and reconciliations before new systems. Kestrel & Pine's four incidents sat on these four paths: the Three-Status Order (#1052877, December 2026: three statuses for six days, eleven tickets), the Double Refund (January 2027: 212 returns, €19,400 refunded twice), the ASN Chargeback (Q3 2026: €14,200 in deductions) and the Black Friday Oversell (27 November 2026: 1,340 units, 1,120 orders, about €96,000). Of Waypoint's eight decisions, three add a system (the availability service, the OMS and the PIM), while its integration standards, its EDI rules and its single definition of an order set owners, contracts, idempotency keys, reconciliations and the source of the despatch advice; the 2027 peak plan is mostly gauges and switches with owners.
thesis.how_why: Each system keeps its own fact on its own clock (checkout in seconds, the warehouse in pick waves, the carrier overnight, the ERP in a daily batch, the bank in days) and learns the other systems' facts as copies, through messages that arrive at least once and sometimes twice, late or not at all. A step can therefore be right in its own system and wrong at the next: a stock copy two hours old, a refund written by two systems, a despatch advice written before the pallets were packed, a queue nobody measured. Running the same dates and amounts through the January 2027 landscape and the late-2027 design holds the main systems constant (the shop platform, the WMS, the ERP, the PSP and the carriers all stay) and changes only owners and joins, which shows that the failures were in the joins.

supporting_claims.claim: A consumer order crosses about fifteen handoffs among eight systems that each hold a piece of it; it holds when each fact (product, price, physical stock, sellable stock, order, payment, parcel, invoice) has one system of record, the order number is the idempotency key on every join, and stock and orders move by event while invoices and payouts move by daily batch under a reconciliation.

A return is three flows with three owners (the goods through the warehouse's inspection, the money through the payment provider, the books through a credit note in the ERP), released by one event, the warehouse's disposition; the refund has one writer and one key, and an exchange is a return plus a new order at the original frozen price.

A wholesale order is a chain of contractual documents, each written by the system that knows the fact it states: the order record by the OMS, keyed on the buyer's location number and purchase-order number; the despatch advice by the warehouse system from the pallets as packed; the invoice by the ERP from the shipped lines. E-invoicing mandates change an invoice's format and transport, not its owner.

Under peak load the chain fails at the links nobody measured: a queue that hides a growing backlog and stock copied on a schedule. A peak plan sets a capacity figure per link, tests it with marked orders, gauges and alarms the queue, sends stock as events, and gives each degradation switch an owner and a trigger, while checkout, payment and the order path are never switched off.

Run on the same dates through the January 2027 landscape (and Black Friday 2026 for the peak), each journey breaks at a handoff where a fact had two writers or no owner, a message had no key or a link had no gauge, while every system did what it was built to do.

flow.rationale: The page opens on one puzzle (a warehouse that reports a parcel shipped while the storefront shows it being prepared, each right about its own fact) and states at once what following orders across the handoffs shows: every journey broke at a handoff, and what makes one hold. It then narrows to the four stories that show it; to the setting they are told in and how each chapter is laid out (the late-2027 design, each chapter ending on the January 2027 landscape, the peak told as Black Friday 2026 and then the 2027 plan); to the one rule of style the comparison pictures (events for stock and orders, a daily batch for finance), beside Figure 3; then one paragraph per chapter; it ends on the opening's parcel as a question to check and where to begin. The claim follows the hook directly because both round-1 flow readers read it as the answer to the hook and the relay figure, and found it unclear after the method; the stories come before the setting because the setting is a property of the stories; the event-and-batch rule comes after the setting because it contrasts the two architectures the setting names. Put the setting first and the reader meets three time frames before knowing what they are for; put the chapter list before the setting and the January comparison each chapter ends with is unexplained.

(house format, kept); a lead of 2–4 paragraphs placing the part, naming Kestrel & Pine as fictional once, saying how to read and that the journeys are set in late 2027 (now p01 to p05; its outcome is AC-2); one or two mermaid diagrams (obsolete since they were redrawn as illustrations on 2026-11-07); the chapter-list format (kept; its outcome is AC-1); every number matching the chapters and the ledger (checked at conversion, see changelog); no Across Scale Stages and a one-line Sources and Evidence (kept).
rejected: Carrying the checklist over as acceptance criteria: they say what the page contains, not what a reader can do.

decision_log.decision: Figure 1 draws the four journeys entering one shared chain of systems through four doors, rather than one journey's sequence, because 'same systems, different door' is what the four chapters share. (Carried from spec.md; the figure is now Figure 2, beside the four stories.)

Figure 2 draws the January 2027 chain against the late-2027 chain, because the 'before Waypoint' comparison is the reading device the lead promises. (Carried from spec.md; now Figure 3, beside the claim.)

Four failure patterns: Schrödinger's Order and The Message in a Bottle (every journey), The Phantom Stock (Journeys 1, 3 and 4) and The First Snowfall (Journey 4). (Carried from spec.md; the FAILURE PATTERNS block was dropped on 2026-11-08.)
The lead says the first three journeys share one shape and the fourth is told twice, so a reader is not surprised when Journey 4 has no step table. (Carried from spec.md.)
